questions.q: What is a biodiversity hotspot, and which hotspots are found in India?

answer.text: A biodiversity hotspot, a concept given by Norman Myers, is a region that is exceptionally rich in life yet is seriously threatened. To qualify, a region must have very high endemism, with at least fifteen hundred species of endemic plants found nowhere else, and it must have lost at least seventy per cent of its original natural habitat. Hotspots are therefore priority areas for conservation, since they hold much of the world's biodiversity in small, endangered areas.

India contains four biodiversity hotspots. These are the Himalayas in the north, the Western Ghats together with Sri Lanka along the south-west, the Indo-Burma region in the north-east, and Sundaland, which includes the Nicobar group of islands.
These regions harbour a wealth of endemic and endangered species and demand urgent protection.

answer: Thus hotspots identify the most valuable and vulnerable areas of biodiversity for conservation.

questions.q: Why is the conservation of biodiversity important for human survival?

answer.text: is the variety of life, and conserving it is vital for human well-being and survival.

list: It provides direct goods — food, medicines, timber, fibre and fuel
It provides services — pollination of crops, purification of air and water, and formation of soil
A rich variety of species makes ecosystems more productive and better able to withstand disturbance
Beyond use, biodiversity has ethical and aesthetic value — every species has a right to exist, and we owe it to future generations to protect it

questions.q: What are the main threats to biodiversity today?

answer.text: is being lost at an alarming rate, mainly because of human activities, summed up as 'the evil quartet'.

list: Habitat loss and fragmentation — clearing forests and wetlands destroys the homes of species
Over-exploitation — hunting and over-harvesting drive species to extinction
Invasive alien species out-compete and wipe out native species
Co-extinctions, where the loss of one species drags down others linked to it, and pollution and climate change worsen the crisis
